title: Bayes' Theorem
hook: A treasure-hunt story and a Nobel-Prize-winning psychological puzzle are used to frame the formula as urgently practical before any math appears.

scenes.purpose: Establish stakes and promise three levels of understanding, tackled in reverse order

on_screen.desc: Levels of Understanding list with three nested bubble icons in gradient green→red
Bayes formula tucked in corner, Pi-creature reacting
Science / robot / gold-bar icons representing applications

scenes.transition: Formula shrinks to corner; levels list fades; Steve character appears upper-right
scenes.narration_gist: Before dissecting the formula, we tackle its usefulness first by meeting Steve.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the Steve description and surface the intuitive (wrong) snap judgment

on_screen.desc: Steve SVG figure with name label
Personality description paragraph with 'meek and tidy soul' highlighted yellow
Probability bar animating between Librarian and Farmer ends

scenes.transition: Description fades; bar and Steve remain as Kahneman/Tversky photos slide in
scenes.narration_gist: Most people say Steve is more likely a librarian because the description matches the stereotype.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the missing prior — the farmer-to-librarian ratio — as the crux of the error

on_screen.desc: One Librarian figure next to 20 Farmer figures arranged in a row
Brace over farmers labeled '20', brace over librarian labeled '1'
Kahneman and Tversky portrait photos (then fade out)

scenes.transition: Row of people shrinks into a bounding rectangle; colored sub-rectangles overlay it
scenes.narration_gist: The 20-to-1 ratio of farmers to librarians is the prior that people ignore.

scenes.purpose: Work through the representative-sample calculation that secretly IS Bayes' theorem

on_screen.desc: Big rectangle split left (librarians) / right (farmers); colored bands show who fits description
Equation P(Librarian | description) = 4 / (4+20) ≈ 16.7%
Brace tracking count of matching librarians (4) and farmers (20)

scenes.transition: People figures fade; equation persists; prior-label arrow slides in above fraction
scenes.narration_gist: Even though librarians are four times more likely to fit the description, there are so many more farmers that only 16.7% of matches are librarians.

scenes.purpose: Name the formula parts — prior, likelihood, posterior — and crystallise the mantra

on_screen.desc: Labelled call-outs: 'Prior', 'Likelihood', 'P(E|¬H)' with color-coded arrows
Expanded Bayes formula with numerator and denominator terms highlighted
Italic mantra: 'New evidence updates prior beliefs'

scenes.transition: Expanded denominator collapses to P(E); 'Posterior' label added; formula shrinks to top-left corner
scenes.narration_gist: Each piece of the formula has a name — prior, likelihood, posterior — and together they formalise the updating of beliefs.

scenes.purpose: Show the geometric diagram as a re-derivable visual substitute for memorising the formula

on_screen.desc: 1×1 square split vertically by prior P(H), left band yellow, right grey
Restricted diagram with horizontal evidence bands; faded non-evidence strips
Geometric fraction: blue he_rect over (he_rect + nhe_rect) with line between

scenes.transition: Both diagrams animate prior and likelihood sliders; 'Write this more mathematically' label prompts return to formula
scenes.narration_gist: The 1×1 square diagram lets you re-derive Bayes' theorem on the fly using areas instead of counts.

scenes.purpose: Linda problem — show how frequency framing eliminates a 85% error rate

on_screen.desc: Linda description text with bank-teller options listed
85% statistic highlighted in red, then rephrased as 'out of 100 people…'
Nested set diagram: bank tellers containing feminist bank-teller subset

scenes.transition: Linda panel fades; return to Bayes square diagram with slider animation
scenes.narration_gist: Rephrasing from probability to frequency (40 out of 100) nearly eliminates the conjunction fallacy, showing that concrete counts activate better intuition.

scenes.purpose: Reframe probability as proportions/geometry and show the formula is 'obvious' once visualised

on_screen.desc: Bayes square with both evidence bands visible and labeled
Full Bayes formula with geometric reading: width × height = area of rectangle
Text: 'Both sides look at cases where evidence is true'

scenes.transition: Formula and diagram persist side by side; debate about Steve context introduced via text overlay
scenes.narration_gist: Probability is really just the math of proportions, and the diagram makes Bayes' theorem geometrically obvious.

scenes.purpose: Close with Steve revisited and the meta-lesson about reprogramming intuition

on_screen.desc: Steve figure in corner
Discussion: ambiguous context shifts the prior; stereotypes shift likelihoods
Final mantra: 'Evidence should update beliefs, not determine them'

scenes.transition: All elements fade; clean frame holds the closing sentence
scenes.narration_gist: Whether or not Kahneman's specific experiment convinces you, the core principle — evidence updates priors — is worth internalising deeply.

lessons: Open with a concrete human story before introducing any notation; let stakes justify the abstraction.
Introduce the visual diagram before the algebraic formula so the formula reads as a description of something already understood.
Use color-coding that persists across every representation — diagram, formula, labels — so viewers track the same concept across transitions without re-reading.
Replace abstract percentages with counts ('4 out of 24') when building intuition, then generalise to proportions only after the concrete case is secure.
Keep one anchor object (the Bayes square) on screen across multiple scenes and animate its parameters so viewers see the formula as a living, adjustable thing rather than a static symbol.
Name every formula part exactly once, with a label and arrow, then drop the label and trust the established color to carry the meaning forward.
tags: bayes probability evidence hypothesis update prior likelihood
